notes.definition: The percentage yield compares the amount of product actually obtained with the maximum theoretical amount that could be made, calculated from the balanced equation: percentage yield = (mass of product actually made ÷ maximum theoretical mass of product) × 100.
explanation: Even though no atoms are gained or lost in a chemical reaction, it is not always possible to obtain the calculated amount of a product. The amount of product actually collected is called the actual yield. The largest amount that could possibly be made, if every bit of the limiting reactant turned into the product, is the maximum theoretical mass (the theoretical yield). The percentage yield tells you how close the actual yield is to the theoretical yield.

Percentage yield = mass of product actually made ÷ maximum theoretical mass of product × 100. A yield of 100% would mean no product was lost at all, which almost never happens. For example, if a reaction could make 8.0 g of product but only 6.0 g is collected, the percentage yield is 6.0 ÷ 8.0 × 100 = 75%. Make sure both masses are in the same unit before dividing.

There are three main reasons why the yield is less than 100%. First, the reaction may not go to completion because it is reversible: some products turn back into reactants, so an equilibrium mixture forms. Second, some of the product may be lost when it is separated from the reaction mixture, for example left on filter paper, left in the beaker or lost during transfer between containers, or when crystals are dried. Third, some of the reactants may react in ways different from the expected reaction, forming unwanted side products.

Higher tier students must be able to calculate the theoretical mass of product from a given mass of reactant and the balanced equation, using the moles method: convert the mass of reactant to moles, use the mole ratio to find moles of product, then convert to mass. For example, 50 g of calcium carbonate (0.50 mol) can make at most 0.50 mol of calcium oxide, which is 28 g. If 22.4 g is collected, the percentage yield is 22.4 ÷ 28 × 100 = 80%.

A high percentage yield matters in industry. Low yields waste raw materials and energy, cost more money and produce more waste that must be disposed of. Chemists try to improve yields by choosing reaction conditions carefully, recycling unreacted starting materials, and using careful separation techniques. However, the percentage yield is only one factor: the rate of reaction and the atom economy also affect which process is chosen.
keyFacts: Percentage yield = (mass of product actually made ÷ maximum theoretical mass) × 100.
The maximum theoretical mass is calculated from the balanced equation.
Yield is less than 100% because: the reaction may be reversible and not go to completion; product is lost during separation; reactants may take part in unexpected side reactions.
Atoms are still conserved even when the yield is below 100%.
Both masses must be in the same unit before calculating the percentage yield.
(HT) The theoretical mass is found using moles: mass → moles, mole ratio, moles → mass.
A higher percentage yield means less waste of reactants and lower costs.
A percentage yield above 100% suggests the product is impure or still wet.

keyTerms.definition: The amount of product obtained from a reaction.
The mass of product actually collected in an experiment or process.
The maximum mass of product that could be made, calculated from the balanced equation and the mass of limiting reactant.
The actual yield as a percentage of the theoretical yield.
A reaction in which the products can react to re-form the reactants, so it may not go to completion.
An unwanted reaction that turns some reactants into products other than the one wanted.

equations.name: Percentage yield
equations.formula: percentage yield = mass of product actually made ÷ maximum theoretical mass of product × 100

workedExamples.title: Simple percentage yield
workedExamples.question: A student calculates that a reaction should produce 8.0 g of copper sulfate crystals. She collects 6.0 g. Calculate the percentage yield.

workedExamples.title: Rearranging to find the actual mass
workedExamples.question: A process has a percentage yield of 60%. The maximum theoretical mass of product is 25 g. Calculate the mass of product actually made.
steps: Rearrange: actual mass = percentage yield ÷ 100 × theoretical mass.

workedExamples.title: (HT) Calculating the theoretical mass first
workedExamples.question: 50 g of calcium carbonate is heated: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. 22.4 g of calcium oxide is collected. Calculate the percentage yield. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40)
steps: Ratio CaCO₃ : CaO = 1 : 1, so maximum moles of CaO = 0.50 mol.
Maximum theoretical mass of CaO = 0.50 × 56 = 28 g.

workedExamples.title: (HT) Working in kilograms
workedExamples.question: In the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. A reactor converts 28 kg of nitrogen and produces 5.1 kg of ammonia. Calculate the percentage yield. (Ar: H = 1, N = 14)
steps: Mass ratio from the equation: 28 g of N₂ (1 mol) makes 34 g of NH₃ (2 mol × 17).
So 28 kg of N₂ could make 34 kg of NH₃ (same ratio in kg).
The yield is low because the reaction is reversible.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a yield below 100% means atoms have been destroyed.
misconceptions.right: In fact atoms are conserved. The missing product was lost during separation, never formed because the reaction is reversible, or the atoms ended up in side products.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often divide the theoretical yield by the actual yield.
misconceptions.right: In fact percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100. The answer should be 100% or less.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a percentage yield above 100% is a very good result.
misconceptions.right: In fact a yield over 100% shows an error, usually that the product is still wet or contains impurities.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think percentage yield and atom economy measure the same thing.
misconceptions.right: In fact percentage yield compares actual product with the theoretical amount, while atom economy measures what fraction of reactant atoms end up in the desired product according to the equation.

realWorld: The Haber process for ammonia has a low yield on each pass through the reactor because the reaction is reversible, so unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled.
Pharmaceutical companies often make medicines in many steps; a small loss at each step makes the overall yield low, so improving the yield of each step saves a lot of money.
Making copper sulfate crystals in school typically gives yields well below 100% because some solution is left on equipment and some product stays dissolved.
higherTier: Calculate the theoretical mass of a product from a given mass of reactant and the balanced equation for the reaction, then use it to find the percentage yield.
separateOnlyContent: The whole of this subtopic (percentage yield) is in separate Chemistry only, not Combined Science Trilogy.
examTips: Learn the three reasons for yields below 100%: reversible reaction (not complete), product lost in separation, and reactants reacting in unexpected ways.
Check your answer: a percentage yield must be 100% or less. If it is more, you have divided the wrong way round.
In Higher questions, calculate the theoretical mass first, clearly labelled, then use it in the percentage yield equation.
Give specific losses in practical questions, for example 'solution left in the beaker' or 'crystals stuck to filter paper', not just 'human error'.
Keep units consistent: if one mass is in kg and the other in g, convert one of them.
summary: Percentage yield = actual mass ÷ maximum theoretical mass × 100.
Reasons: reversible reactions, product lost in separation, side reactions.
(HT) Theoretical mass is calculated from the equation using moles.
High yields save raw materials, energy and money.
A yield over 100% means the product is impure or wet.

questions.question: Which equation is used to calculate the percentage yield of a reaction?
questions.explanation: Percentage yield = mass actually made ÷ maximum theoretical mass × 100. Dividing the other way gives a value above 100%.

questions.question:
The maximum theoretical mass of product in a reaction is 10 g.
A student collects 7 g of product.
What is the percentage yield?
questions.explanation: 7 ÷ 10 × 100 = 70%. 30% is the percentage lost, and 143% divides the wrong way round.

questions.question: Which is not a reason why the percentage yield of a reaction is less than 100%?
options: Some product is lost when it is filtered
Some reactants react to form a different product
Atoms are destroyed during the reaction
markScheme: 1 mark: atoms are destroyed during the reaction
questions.explanation: Atoms are never destroyed in a chemical reaction. The other three are the reasons given in the specification.

questions.question:
A student makes some crystals. The student calculates a percentage yield of 112%.
What is the most likely reason for this result?
options: The crystals were still wet when weighed
Some crystals were left on the filter paper
markScheme: 1 mark: the crystals were still wet when weighed
questions.explanation: A yield above 100% is impossible for pure, dry product. Water or impurities add extra mass. Losses on filter paper would lower the yield.

questions.question:
The maximum theoretical mass of product in a process is 50 kg.
The percentage yield is 40%.
What mass of product is made?
questions.explanation: Actual = 40 ÷ 100 × 50 = 20 kg. 125 kg comes from dividing 50 by 0.4.

questions.question:
Ammonia is made in the Haber process.
Why is the yield of ammonia low each time the gases pass through the reactor?
options: The reaction is reversible and does not go to completion
Nitrogen does not react at all
markScheme: 1 mark: the reaction is reversible and does not go to completion
questions.explanation: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ reaches equilibrium, so some reactants remain. A catalyst is not used up.

questions.question:
A student makes crystals from a solution.
Which change to the method would most likely increase the percentage yield?
options: Pouring the solution quickly and spilling some
Rinsing the beaker with a little water and adding it to the solution
Heating the crystals until they decompose
markScheme: 1 mark: rinsing the beaker with a little water and adding it to the solution
questions.explanation: Rinsing transfers solution left on the glassware, so less product is lost. The other options lose or destroy product.

questions.question:
Calcium carbonate decomposes when heated:
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
A student heats 10 g of calcium carbonate and obtains 4.2 g of calcium oxide.
What is the percentage yield?
Relative atomic masses (Ar): C = 12; O = 16; Ca = 40
questions.explanation: Theoretical: 0.10 mol CaCO₃ gives 0.10 mol CaO = 5.6 g. 4.2 ÷ 5.6 × 100 = 75%. 42% wrongly uses 10 g as the theoretical mass.

questions.question:
A product is made in two steps.
Table 1 shows the percentage yield of each step.
What is the overall percentage yield?
questions.explanation: Only half of the product of step 1 is carried through step 2: 0.50 × 0.50 = 0.25, so 25%. Yields multiply, not add.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the results of a reaction.
Calculate the percentage yield.
questions.explanation: Percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100 = 75%.

questions.question:
A student makes a salt.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the percentage yield.

A factory could make 1.5 tonnes of product from its raw materials.
The factory actually makes 1.2 tonnes of product.
Calculate the percentage yield.
questions.explanation: Both masses are in tonnes, so no conversion is needed: 1.2 ÷ 1.5 × 100 = 80%.

questions.question:
The maximum theoretical mass of product in a process is 25 g.
The percentage yield is 60%.
Calculate the mass of product actually made.
questions.explanation: Rearrange: actual = percentage yield ÷ 100 × theoretical mass.

questions.question:
A student obtains 18 g of product. The percentage yield is 90%.
Calculate the maximum theoretical mass of product.
questions.explanation: Rearrange: theoretical mass = actual mass × 100 ÷ percentage yield. 18 × 100 ÷ 90 = 20 g.

questions.question:
Calcium carbonate decomposes when heated:
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂
Table 1 shows the results of an experiment.
Calculate the percentage yield of calcium oxide.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): C = 12; O = 16; Ca = 40
questions.explanation: Find the theoretical mass from the equation, then compare the actual mass with it.

questions.question:
Magnesium burns in oxygen:
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
Table 1 shows the results of an experiment.
Calculate the percentage yield of magnesium oxide.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): O = 16; Mg = 24
questions.explanation: Some magnesium oxide smoke escapes, or not all the magnesium reacts, so the yield is below 100%.

questions.question:
The equation for the Haber process is:
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃
28 kg of nitrogen reacts and 5.1 kg of ammonia is produced.
Calculate the percentage yield of ammonia.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): H = 1; N = 14
markScheme: 1 mark: 28 kg N₂ (1000 mol) gives 2000 mol NH₃
questions.explanation: 1 mol of N₂ (28 g) can make 2 mol of NH₃ (34 g), so 28 kg could make 34 kg. The reaction is reversible, so the yield is low.

questions.question:
Copper oxide reacts with excess sulfuric acid:
CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O
Table 1 shows the results of an experiment.
Calculate the percentage yield of copper sulfate.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): O = 16; S = 32; Cu = 63.5
questions.explanation: Copper oxide is the limiting reactant because the acid is in excess, so use it to find the theoretical mass.

questions.question: What is meant by the percentage yield of a reaction?
acceptedAnswers: actual yield as a percentage of theoretical yield
markScheme: 1 mark: the mass of product actually made as a percentage of the maximum theoretical mass
questions.explanation: It compares what you got with what you could have got.

questions.question: Give three reasons why it is not always possible to obtain the calculated amount of a product.
markScheme: 1 mark: the reaction may not go to completion because it is reversible
1 mark: some product may be lost when it is separated from the reaction mixture
1 mark: some reactants may react in ways different from the expected reaction
questions.explanation: These are the three reasons named in the AQA specification.

questions.question: Explain why chemical companies want reactions with a high percentage yield.
markScheme: 1 mark: less of the reactants (raw materials) are wasted
1 mark: so costs are lower / less energy used / less waste to dispose of / more sustainable
questions.explanation: A higher yield means more product for the same amount of raw materials and energy.

questions.question:
A student calculates a percentage yield of 105%.
Suggest two reasons for this result.
markScheme: 1 mark: the product was not completely dry (contained water)
1 mark: the product contained impurities (or an error in weighing or calculating the theoretical mass)
questions.explanation: Real yields cannot exceed 100% for a pure, dry product, so extra mass must come from something else.

questions.question:
Sodium reacts with excess chlorine:
2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl
Table 1 shows the results of an experiment.
Calculate the percentage yield of sodium chloride.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): Na = 23; Cl = 35.5
markScheme: 1 mark: moles Na = 0.20, so moles NaCl = 0.20
questions.explanation: Sodium is limiting, so it determines the theoretical mass of 11.7 g.

questions.question:
A student reacts copper oxide with sulfuric acid to make copper sulfate crystals.
The maximum theoretical mass of copper sulfate crystals is 5.0 g. The student collects 3.5 g.
Calculate the percentage yield.
Explain why the percentage yield is less than 100%.
markScheme: Indicative content: 3.5 ÷ 5.0 × 100 = 70%; some solution left in the beaker or on glassware; some lost on filter paper during filtration; some copper sulfate stays dissolved in the solution after crystallisation; spillage during transfers; not all the copper oxide may have reacted; atoms are not destroyed.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct percentage yield with at least two specific, well-explained reasons.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): correct calculation or one reason given.
questions.explanation: 70%. In a practical like this, most losses happen during filtering, transferring and crystallising.

questions.question:
Iron is extracted from iron(III) oxide in a blast furnace:
Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
Table 1 shows information about the blast furnace.
Calculate the percentage yield of iron.
Suggest reasons why the yield is less than 100%.
Explain why improving the yield is important to the company and to the environment.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): O = 16; Fe = 56
markScheme: Indicative content: Mr Fe₂O₃ = 160; 160 tonnes of Fe₂O₃ gives 112 tonnes of Fe; 800 tonnes gives 560 tonnes (or moles method: 800 000 000 g ÷ 160 = 5 000 000 mol, Fe = 10 000 000 mol × 56 = 560 tonnes); percentage yield = 504 ÷ 560 × 100 = 90%; reasons: some iron oxide does not react; some iron lost in slag or when tapped from furnace; side reactions; ore impure. Importance: less raw material mined; less energy and fuel used per tonne of iron; less carbon dioxide emitted per tonne; lower cost and more profit; less waste.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): correct calculation with clear working (90%), sensible reasons for losses and a clear explanation of economic and environmental benefits.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): theoretical mass or percentage yield correct, with some reasons or benefits.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): an attempt at the calculation or a simple reason or benefit.
questions.explanation: The theoretical mass is 560 tonnes, so the yield is 90%. Improving yield reduces mining, energy use and carbon dioxide emissions per tonne of iron, as well as cost.
